title: Langtang Lirung rock-ice collapse, 26 Aug 2026
site_label: Collapse deposit (centre of the coherence loss)

story.see: On 26 August 2026 a huge piece of the north face of Langtang Lirung, on the Nepal-China border, collapsed. The seismic signal was recorded at 02:52 UTC (USGS and GFZ, as summarised on Wikipedia). The orange patch is where the radar picture between NISAR's 19 and 31 August passes changed completely compared with an earlier quiet pair (14 to 26 July): the surface was rearranged, so the two passes can no longer be compared there. In the coherence layer a thin dark line also runs from the patch down the valley to the south-west.
story.physics: A rock-ice avalanche throws a huge mass of debris onto the valley floor, burying and churning the surface. Radar does not see the rock itself; it sees that the tiny details of the ground no longer match. The loss of coherence is concentrated in about 8 square kilometres around 28.32 N, 85.48 E, a few kilometres from the location given in published descriptions of the event (north of Langtang Lirung). ICIMOD's preliminary estimate of the detached volume is 132 million cubic metres; we do not measure volume.
story.lband: NISAR's L-band radar has a wavelength of about 24 cm, so it keeps its grip on snow, rock and soil that shorter wavelengths lose within days. That is why this mountain scene is mostly well matched between passes and the collapse stands out so sharply. In the same pair taken 5 weeks earlier on the same track nothing like this exists. The descending track (16 to 28 August) shows the same patch at the same place.
story.people: This map shows where the ground surface changed, not damage. We did not look at reports of damage or casualties. Steep mountain geometry distorts radar images, so we only claim the loss of coherence, not the size of the deposit or the path of the flood.

extra_spots.label: Largest patch of lost coherence (about 8 km2)

verdict_reason: 8.5 km2 patch at 28.32 N 85.48 E, 4.7x the next largest, both look directions

title: Kilauea summit eruption, episode 55, 17 Oct 2026

story.see: Kilauea's summit has been erupting in short bursts called episodes. Episode 55 was on 17 October 2026: about 6 hours of lava fountaining up to 220 m high, with lava also overflowing the vents beforehand (USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory, preliminary). The orange area is where the radar picture between NISAR's 10 and 22 October passes no longer matches the quieter pair before it (28 September to 10 October). It covers the crater and a band to the south-west.
story.physics: Fresh lava and the ash and fine glass it throws out have a completely different surface from what the radar saw before, so the radar echoes no longer match. About 8 square kilometres within 4 km of the crater lost coherence (10 in the largest connected patch); the south-west band lies in the direction the trade winds usually carry ash, but we cannot tell lava from fallout. HVO reports 7 million cubic metres of lava for this episode; we do not measure volume.
story.lband: NISAR's L-band radar has a wavelength of about 24 cm. Over most of this volcano it keeps a good match between passes, so a patch that loses it stands out. The earlier pair has no such patch outside the crater, and over the rest of the map less than 0.5 % of the comparable ground behaves like this. Ground motion (fringes) is not used here: the signal within 4 km is no larger than the noise of the earlier pair.
story.people: This map shows where the surface changed, not damage. We did not look at reports of damage or casualties. Other episodes (53 on 12 August, 54 on 25 August) fall in other pairs and could be shown the same way.

extra_spots.label: Centre of the largest patch of lost coherence

verdict_reason: 10.2 km2 patch in and south-west of Halemaumau, 8.4 km2 within 4 km vs background p95 0.44 km2 (ascending only; descending pair too noisy)

title: Etna eruption and Valle del Bove lava field, Jul-Aug 2026

story.see: Mount Etna in Sicily had a week of lava fountains and lava flows in early August 2026; on 13 August it was in its seventh day, with several vents feeding a lava field in the Valle del Bove (Euronews, citing INGV). The orange patch is where the radar picture between NISAR's 23 July and 16 August passes changed completely compared with the 24 days before (29 June to 23 July). It is a strip about 5 km long running east from the summit craters.
story.physics: Fresh lava has a completely new surface, so the radar no longer matches the earlier picture there. The patch covers about 2.5 square kilometres (3.2 in the whole window); in the whole rest of the 40 km window almost nothing behaves like this. The pair spans 24 days, so it includes the 30 July summit paroxysm as well as the August lava, and we cannot separate them. Older flows already dark before 23 July are not counted.
story.lband: NISAR's L-band radar has a wavelength of about 24 cm. Over most of Etna it keeps a good match between passes, which makes new lava, which scrambles the surface, easy to pick out. The control pair of equal length (29 June to 23 July) shows no such patch. The descending track (23 July to 16 August) shows the same strip, about 2 km2, at the same place.
story.people: This map shows where the surface changed, not damage or the full extent of the lava, which can be thinner or hidden from the radar by steep slopes. We did not look at reports of damage. The product is provisional.

verdict_reason: 2.5 km2 strip east of the summit craters in the ascending pair; 1.2 + 1.0 km2 at the same place in the descending pair; 0.02 % of comparable ground elsewhere
time_note: start of the August eruption inferred from 'seventh day' on 13 Aug (Euronews); the 24-day pair also holds the 30 Jul paroxysm

Thunder Bay 36 fire, Ontario: forest surface changed over 1,500 km2, 11-23 July 2026
time_note: fire started 12 Jul; pair 11-23 Jul; the control pair ends the day before
verdict_reason: sharp-edged patch of lost coherence 1,253 km2 connected (1,540 km2 in the window, cut by the window edge), in both look directions at the published fire; control coherence 0.66 -> 0.13 on those pixels; the same ground is coherent again in the 21 Sep-3 Oct pair; null check: 29 Jun-11 Jul vs 17-29 Jun gives 11.7 km2 in the whole window

extra_spots.label: Centre of the largest patch of lost coherence

story.see: Thunder Bay 36 started on 12 July 2026 in Wabakimi Provincial Park, north-western Ontario, and was about 314,000 hectares (3,140 km2) on 29 July, the largest wildfire in the province's recorded history (Wikipedia, citing the provincial figures). The orange area is where the radar picture between NISAR's 11 and 23 July passes no longer matches the pair taken just before it (29 June to 11 July). It forms a sharp-edged blotch tens of kilometres across, far larger than the 40 x 40 km box the pair was cut to.
story.physics: A fire changes the ground the radar sees: leaves, twigs and the litter on the ground burn or fall, so the tiny details that made the echo repeatable disappear. In the window about 1,540 km2 lost coherence (the biggest connected patch is 1,253 km2), at 50.65 N 89.29 W, 14 km from the published fire point. The ascending pass (track 47) sees a similar patch where its swath covers the area. We do not measure the burned area: the patch is cut by the window and the fire kept growing after 23 July.
story.lband: NISAR's L-band radar (wavelength about 24 cm) normally keeps a good match between two passes 12 days apart over boreal forest, which is why the control pair is largely bright. Lost coherence here has a hard, irregular outline, not the gentle gradient of rain or soil moisture. In the autumn pair (21 September to 3 October) the same ground is coherent again, so the map marks the change that happened inside 11 to 23 July. As a check, the same recipe applied to the pair before it (29 June to 11 July against 17 to 29 June) finds only 12 km2 in the whole window. Rain on the ground in those days cannot be ruled out from coherence alone; the outline and the published fire place and date are what we rely on.
story.people: This map shows where the surface changed, not damage. We did not look at reports of damage, evacuations or casualties. A second, independent look at this fire from the radar brightness is in the separate Thunder Bay 36 place.

verdict_reason: 87 km2 of lost coherence within 12 km (largest patch 43.6 km2, 149 km2 in the window) against a 95th percentile of 13.8 km2 in 98 equal random discs and 1.3 % of comparable ground outside; control 0.79 -> 0.27; the same ground is coherent again on 31 Aug-12 Sep; ascending 7-19 Jul vs 25 Jun-7 Jul: 56 km2 within 12 km (largest patch 25.5 km2 at the same place) vs background p95 0.5 km2

story.see: The La Mierla fire began on 16 July 2026 in the province of Guadalajara, north of Madrid. By 20 July it had burned over 32,000 hectares and was called the second biggest wildfire in Spain this century and the largest in the history of Castilla-La Mancha (The Local). The orange area is where the radar picture between NISAR's 14 and 26 July passes no longer matches the pair taken just before it (2 to 14 July). It is a long band running north-north-east from the village of La Mierla.
story.physics: Burning removes leaves, twigs and scrub, and what is left reflects the radar differently, so the passes cannot be compared there. About 150 km2 in the map lost coherence (87 km2 within 12 km of the centre, 44 km2 in the largest connected patch). Equal circles placed elsewhere in the same map lose at most 14 km2 (95th percentile of 98), and only about 1 % of the comparable ground outside the site changes like this. We do not measure the burned area: the patch only counts ground that was coherent before. The ascending pass (7 to 19 July, control 25 June to 7 July) shows the same band: 56 km2 within 12 km against at most 0.5 km2 in equal circles elsewhere.
story.lband: NISAR's L-band radar has a wavelength of about 24 cm. Over this dry Mediterranean land the quiet pair before the fire is bright almost everywhere, so a burn stands out as a dark scar with a hard edge. In the pair of 31 August to 12 September the same ground is coherent again (nothing like this patch remains), so the map marks the change that happened inside 14 to 26 July. Dew or rain on the ground cannot be fully excluded from coherence alone; the shape, the place and the date are what we rely on.
story.people: This map shows where the surface changed, not damage. We did not look at reports of damage, evacuations or casualties.

story.see: The Gironde megafire began on Wednesday 22 July 2026 between Saumos and Le Porge and crossed the pine forest towards Lacanau and Lege-Cap-Ferret; the prefecture gave 42,000 hectares burned on 30 July (AFP, via Paris Match Belgium). The orange area is where the radar picture between NISAR's 17 July and 10 August passes no longer matches the pair taken just before it (5 to 17 July). It is a single large patch in the forest, with the Atlantic and the Arcachon basin dark in both pictures.
story.physics: Fire strips the pine canopy and the litter beneath it, and the radar echo of that ground stops repeating. About 334 km2 in the map lost coherence, 261 km2 in one connected patch. Equal circles placed elsewhere in the same map lose at most 40 km2 (95th percentile of 39). The descending pass (14 to 26 July, 12 days) shows a smaller patch at the same forest, 31 km2 within 12 km; its water- and marsh-rich surface keeps less coherence to begin with. We do not measure the burned area; only ground that was coherent before is counted.
story.lband: NISAR's L-band radar has a wavelength of about 24 cm and sees through much of a forest canopy, so a burned forest changes its echo strongly. The pair is 24 days long against a 12-day control, which lowers coherence everywhere a little. In the pair of 22 August to 3 September, after the fire, nothing like this patch remains, so the map marks the change inside 17 July to 10 August. Rain or soil moisture cannot be fully excluded from coherence alone; the shape, the place and the date are what we rely on.
story.people: This map shows where the surface changed, not damage. We did not look at reports of damage, evacuations or casualties.

story.see: The Niebla fire was declared on a Thursday, probably 6 August 2026, in the province of Huelva and crossed into Seville; by 13 August it had burned more than 31,000 hectares, with a perimeter of about 120 km (Infobae). The orange area is where the radar picture between NISAR's 21 July and 14 August passes no longer matches the pair taken just before it (9 to 21 July). It forms a wide sharp-edged block north-east of Niebla.
story.physics: Burning removes the leaves, twigs and scrub that gave this dry hill country a repeatable radar echo. About 218 km2 in the map lost coherence (110 km2 within 15 km of the centre, 50 km2 in the largest connected piece). Equal circles placed elsewhere in the same map lose at most 29 km2. We do not measure the burned area: only ground that was coherent before is counted, and the scar continues outside the map. The ascending pass (same dates, track 15) shows the same block: 145 km2 within 15 km, 113 km2 in the largest piece, against at most 7 km2 in equal circles elsewhere. The pair of 14 to 26 August, after the fire, shows nothing (the scar is coherent again).
story.lband: NISAR's L-band radar has a wavelength of about 24 cm.
